definition:
Scripture speaks of a created world larger than the one we see. Alongside human beings, God made spiritual creatures: angels who serve him, worship him, and carry his messages, and a company of rebel powers led by the one Scripture calls Satan, the adversary and accuser. All of them are creatures. None is God's rival or equal, and none acts outside the limits God sets. The Bible's interest in them is not curiosity about the unseen but the story of God's rule: angels serve God's purposes and his people, the hostile powers oppose them and enslave humanity through sin, deception, and fear of death, and the New Testament proclaims that Christ has disarmed those powers through his cross and will finally destroy them. This study follows that story through the canon. The Nicene Creed confesses God as maker of all things visible and invisible, and the church has consistently read the invisible things as including the angels; the details of their nature and ranks, by contrast, are matters on which Scripture says little.

The Hebrew mal'akh and the Greek angelos both mean ‘messenger’. Both are used of human messengers, as when Jacob sends messengers to Esau (Genesis 32:3) or Mark applies Malachi's promise, “I will send My messenger” (Mark 1:2), to John the Baptist, so the word names a task rather than a kind of being. Augustine made this point: ‘angel’ is the name of an office, ‘spirit’ the name of a nature. Other terms describe heavenly beings by their role or appearance: the cherubim (keruvim), guardians of God's holy presence; the seraphim (serafim, from a root meaning ‘to burn’), seen in Isaiah's vision; the ‘sons of God’ (benei ha'elohim) of Job and Genesis 6; the ‘host’ (tsava') of heaven; ‘holy ones’ (qedoshim) and ‘watchers’ ('irin) in the Psalms and Daniel. The Hebrew satan means ‘adversary’ or ‘accuser’ and can describe human opponents (1 Kings 11:14) or even the angel of the LORD standing ‘to oppose’ Balaam (Numbers 22:22). In Job 1 to 2 and Zechariah 3 it appears with the article, ha-satan, ‘the accuser’. The Septuagint translated it with diabolos, ‘slanderer’, from which comes the English ‘devil’. The New Testament adds ‘the evil one’ (ho ponēros), ‘demons’ (daimonia) or ‘unclean spirits’, and a vocabulary of ‘rulers’ (archai), ‘authorities’ (exousiai), ‘powers’ (dynameis), ‘dominions’, and ‘thrones’.
ot:
The Old Testament never gives an account of the angels' creation, but it counts them among God's creatures. The Psalms call on “all His angels” and “all His heavenly hosts” to praise the LORD, “for He gave the command and they were created” (Psalm 148:2, 5), and God asks Job where he was when “all the sons of God shouted for joy” at the founding of the earth (Job 38:7). In Genesis the tempter is a creature, “the serpent,” “more crafty than any beast of the field that the LORD God had made” (Genesis 3:1). Genesis does not call it Satan; the later canon makes that identification, calling the devil “that ancient serpent” (Revelation 12:9), and God's word that the woman's seed “will crush your head” (Genesis 3:15) became the first hint of a victory over the enemy. After the fall God stations cherubim to guard the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24), and golden cherubim later overshadow the mercy seat of the ark (Exodus 25:20). The strange episode of “the sons of God” taking wives from “the daughters of men” (Genesis 6:1-4) has been read as angels, as the godly line of Seth, or as ancient kings; the views are set out below. Angels appear at key points of the patriarchal story: Jacob dreams of “God's angels” going up and down a stairway to heaven (Genesis 28:12), and later “the angels of God met him” (Genesis 32:1).

A distinctive figure is “the angel of the LORD.” He finds Hagar in the desert, speaks God's promises in the first person, and she names “the LORD who had spoken to her” as “the God who sees me” (Genesis 16:7-13). At the burning bush “the angel of the LORD appeared” and then “God called out to him from within the bush” (Exodus 3:2, 4). God promises to send an angel ahead of Israel of whom he says, “My Name is in him” (Exodus 23:21). A commander of the LORD's army tells Joshua to remove his sandals on holy ground (Joshua 5:13-15), and Manoah, after the angel ascends in the altar flame, says, “we have seen God” (Judges 13:22). The same angel defends God's people (Psalm 34:7) and strikes down the Assyrian army besieging Jerusalem (2 Kings 19:35). Who this figure is has been debated since the early church; the main answers are set out below.

The Old Testament also pictures God surrounded by a heavenly court. The prophet Micaiah sees “the LORD sitting on His throne, and all the host of heaven standing by Him,” and a spirit volunteers to entice Ahab through lying prophets, with God's permission (1 Kings 22:19-22). Psalm 89 speaks of “the council of the holy ones” (Psalm 89:7), and Psalm 82 of God judging “among the gods” in the divine assembly, a psalm read by some as addressing human judges and by others as addressing heavenly beings who ruled unjustly. In Job the sons of God come before the LORD, and among them is ha-satan, the accuser, who questions whether Job fears God “for nothing” (Job 1:9) and can act against Job only within limits God sets (Job 1:12; 2:6). In Zechariah the accuser stands at the high priest's right hand, and the LORD rebukes him (Zechariah 3:1-2). When the two accounts of David's census are compared, what Samuel describes as God's anger stirring David, Chronicles describes as Satan inciting him (2 Samuel 24:1; 1 Chronicles 21:1), where ‘Satan’ appears without the article, perhaps already as a name. Deuteronomy's Song of Moses says that God divided the nations “according to the number of the sons of God” (Deuteronomy 32:8). That is the reading of a Dead Sea Scroll of Deuteronomy and of the Septuagint, which the BSB follows; the traditional Hebrew text reads ‘sons of Israel’. The same song says Israel “sacrificed to demons, not to God” (Deuteronomy 32:17), linking idolatry with hostile spirits, a link the psalms and Paul repeat (Psalm 106:37; 1 Corinthians 10:20).

The prophets add vision and names. Isaiah sees seraphim above God's throne, covering their faces and crying, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts” (Isaiah 6:3), and one of them purifies his lips with a coal from the altar. Isaiah's taunt against the king of Babylon, “How you have fallen from heaven, O day star, son of the dawn” (Isaiah 14:12), and Ezekiel's lament over the king of Tyre as a “guardian cherub” who was “in Eden” until “wickedness was found in you” (Ezekiel 28:13-15) are addressed to human kings; Origen and many later Christian writers heard in them the fall of Satan behind those kings, while many modern interpreters read them as poetic images of royal pride drawing on older myths. The Latin Vulgate rendered ‘day star’ as lucifer, the source of that later name for the devil. Daniel names angels for the first time: Gabriel, who explains visions (Daniel 8:16; 9:21), and Michael, “one of the chief princes” (Daniel 10:13) and “the great prince who stands watch over your people” (Daniel 12:1). Daniel also speaks of “the prince of the kingdom of Persia” and “the prince of Greece” resisting God's messenger (Daniel 10:13, 20), which suggests that spiritual powers are bound up with the empires of the earth. Between the Testaments, Jewish writings such as 1 Enoch expanded the story of Genesis 6 into an account of rebel ‘watchers’, and Tobit introduced the angel Raphael, while the Sadducees, Luke reports, denied angels and spirits altogether (Acts 23:8).
nt:
Angels frame the Gospel story. Gabriel, who stands “in the presence of God” (Luke 1:19), announces the births of John and Jesus; an angel reassures Joseph in a dream (Matthew 1:20); and “a great multitude of the heavenly host” praises God over the shepherds' fields (Luke 2:13-14). After his baptism Jesus is led into the wilderness “to be tempted by the devil” (Matthew 4:1). The devil quotes Psalm 91's promise of angelic protection to tempt him (Matthew 4:6), Jesus answers with Scripture, and afterward “angels came and ministered to Him” (Matthew 4:11). His ministry is a campaign against the powers. He commands unclean spirits, which recognize him as “the Holy One of God” (Mark 1:24-27). When accused of casting out demons by Beelzebul, he answers that “if I drive out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you,” and compares himself to one who ties up a strong man to plunder his house (Matthew 12:28-29). When the seventy-two return rejoicing, he says, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven,” but tells them to rejoice rather “that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:18, 20). Satan enters Judas (Luke 22:3) and asks to sift Peter like wheat, but Jesus has prayed for him (Luke 22:31-32), a scene that echoes Job. In John's Gospel the devil is “a murderer from the beginning” and “the father of lies” (John 8:44), and as the cross approaches Jesus says, “now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John 12:31).

Jesus also speaks of the holy angels. There is joy “in the presence of God's angels over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15:10). He warns against despising “little ones,” because “their angels in heaven always see the face of My Father” (Matthew 18:10), a saying behind the long Christian belief in guardian angels. In the resurrection people will be “like the angels” in not marrying (Matthew 22:30), which does not say that human beings become angels. He could call on “more than twelve legions of angels” but does not (Matthew 26:53), and at the judgment the unrighteous are sent into “the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41), a fire not made for human beings at all. In Acts angels open prison doors for the apostles (Acts 5:19; 12:7), and Paul's commission is to turn people “from the power of Satan to God” (Acts 26:18).

Paul places every power under Christ. All things were created in the Son, “whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities” (Colossians 1:16), and God seated the risen Christ “far above all rule and authority, power and dominion” (Ephesians 1:21). At the cross God, “having disarmed the powers and authorities,” made “a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them” (Colossians 2:15), an image drawn from a Roman triumphal procession in which defeated enemies were paraded. Nothing, “neither angels nor principalities” nor any powers, can separate believers from God's love in Christ (Romans 8:38-39). The powers are defeated but not yet destroyed. Before conversion believers followed “the ruler of the power of the air” (Ephesians 2:2), “The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers” (2 Corinthians 4:4), and “Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light” (2 Corinthians 11:14). So Paul tells believers to “Put on the full armor of God,” since “our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities” (Ephesians 6:11-12). The armor is truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, and the word of God, with prayer (Ephesians 6:14-18); the weapons are the ordinary gifts of the Christian life. Even Paul's “thorn in my flesh,” which he calls “a messenger of Satan,” served to keep him humble (2 Corinthians 12:7). Paul forbids “the worship of angels” (Colossians 2:18), says that believers “will judge angels” (1 Corinthians 6:3), and promises that “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20), an echo of Genesis 3:15. Scholars debate whether the stoicheia of Galatians 4:3, 9 and Colossians 2:8, 20 are ‘elementary principles’ or ‘elemental spirits’; the BSB renders the word “basic principles” in Galatians and “spiritual forces” in Colossians.

The other letters agree. Hebrews insists that the Son is superior to the angels, whom God commands to worship him (Hebrews 1:6), and that angels are “ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation” (Hebrews 1:14). The Son shared human flesh “so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death” (Hebrews 2:14-15). Peter says that “angels long to look into” the gospel (1 Peter 1:12), that angels and powers are subject to the risen Christ (1 Peter 3:22), and that “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion,” to be resisted in faith (1 Peter 5:8-9). James adds, “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7). Second Peter and Jude speak of angels who sinned and are held for judgment (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 1:6); Peter's verb, tartaroō, borrows the Greek name for the lowest underworld, and many interpreters connect both passages with the Jewish reading of Genesis 6 found in 1 Enoch, which Jude quotes elsewhere (Jude 1:14-15). Jude's account of Michael disputing with the devil over Moses' body (Jude 1:9) was traced by early Christian writers to a Jewish work about Moses' death. John writes that “the Son of God was revealed, to destroy the works of the devil” (1 John 3:8). Revelation shows Michael and his angels casting down “that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan” (Revelation 12:9), and the saints conquer the accuser “by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony” (Revelation 12:11). The devil is finally thrown into the lake of fire (Revelation 20:10). When John falls at an angel's feet, he is told, “Do not do that! I am a fellow servant with you” (Revelation 22:9).

keyTexts.why: A crafty creature deceives the first humans, and God promises that the woman's seed will crush its head. The New Testament identifies the serpent with the devil.
The angel of the LORD speaks God's promises to Hagar, and she names the LORD who spoke to her. The first appearance of a figure whose identity the church has long debated.
The accuser appears among the sons of God and acts against Job only within the limits God sets. Satan is a creature under God's rule, never his equal.
God's kingdom rules over all, and his mighty angels are called to bless him as servants who do his will. Angels exist to worship and obey.
Seraphim cry holy, holy, holy before the enthroned LORD, and one of them cleanses the prophet. Heavenly worship, echoed in the church's liturgy.
God's messenger is opposed by the prince of Persia and helped by Michael. Spiritual conflict is bound up with the history of nations.
The accuser stands against the high priest, and the LORD rebukes him. God's choosing grace silences the accusation.
Jesus meets the devil in the wilderness and overcomes him with Scripture, and angels minister to him. Christ succeeds where Adam and Israel failed.
Jesus casts out demons by the Spirit of God, a sign that the kingdom has come and the strong man is bound. Exorcism as the kingdom's arrival.
Jesus sees Satan fall and tells his disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven. Victory over the enemy matters less than belonging to God.
The church's struggle is against spiritual powers, and its armor is truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, the word, and prayer. The New Testament's fullest account of spiritual conflict.
At the cross God forgave sins and disarmed the powers and authorities, triumphing over them. The heart of the New Testament's teaching on the powers.
The Son sits at God's right hand, and angels are ministering spirits sent to serve the heirs of salvation. Angels are servants, not rivals of Christ.
The devil prowls like a roaring lion, and believers resist him by standing firm in the faith with the worldwide church. Watchfulness without panic.
The dragon is cast down, and the saints conquer the accuser by the blood of the Lamb and their testimony. The victory of the cross pictured in heaven and on earth.

history:
The early church took angels and demons for granted and gave them a clear place in its confession. The Nicene Creed (325, expanded 381) confesses God as maker of all things visible and invisible, which the fathers read as including the angels, so that no spiritual being exists that God did not make. Candidates for baptism renounced the devil and his angels; Tertullian mentions the practice in The Crown (about 211), and it survives in baptismal rites today. Many second-century writers, including Justin Martyr, read Genesis 6 as the fall of angels, following 1 Enoch, while later writers such as Julius Africanus and Augustine read the sons of God as the line of Seth. Athanasius's Life of Antony (about 360) portrayed the desert monk's long struggle with demons and his confidence that they are powerless before Christ, and it shaped monastic spirituality for centuries. Augustine, in The City of God (books 11 and 12), taught that the angels were created good, that some fell by turning from God in pride, and that the two cities of his great work, the city of God and the earthly city, began among the angels. Origen's speculations, that spiritual beings fell from a prior state to varying degrees and that even the devil might one day be restored, were rejected in anathemas against Origenist teaching associated with the Second Council of Constantinople (553). Against dualist teachers who made the devil an independent principle of evil, the First Council of Braga (561) condemned the claim that the devil was not first created a good angel by God.

The medieval church systematized the doctrine. The writings attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite, composed around 500, arranged the angels in nine orders in three groups (seraphim, cherubim, and thrones; dominions, powers, and authorities; principalities, archangels, and angels), a scheme Gregory the Great also used and that shaped art and poetry, including Dante's Paradiso. The Fourth Lateran Council (1215) confessed that God created from nothing both spiritual and bodily creatures, angelic and earthly, and that the devil and the other demons were created good by nature and became evil by their own doing. Anselm of Canterbury's On the Fall of the Devil (around 1085 to 1090) examined how a creature made good could will evil, and Thomas Aquinas, later called the Angelic Doctor, treated the angels at length in the Summa Theologiae (first part, questions 50 to 64), teaching that they are pure intellects without bodies.

The Reformers kept the doctrine but pruned speculation. John Calvin, in the Institutes (Book 1, chapter 14), taught that angels are God's ministers for the good of believers and that the devil is a real enemy under God's control, while warning against the idle curiosity he found in the Dionysian hierarchies. Martin Luther's hymn A Mighty Fortress (around 1529) sang of the devil's rage and his defeat by a single word, and his Small Catechism (1529) gave morning and evening prayers asking that God's holy angel be with the one praying. The Belgic Confession (1561, article 12) confesses that God created the angels good, that some fell and became enemies of God and humanity, and rejects both the Sadducees, who deny spirits, and the Manichees, who make the devil self-originating. The Western church kept the feast of Saint Michael and All Angels on 29 September, and the Roman Rite of exorcism, issued in 1614, was revised in 1999. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992, paragraphs 328 to 336 and 391 to 395) calls the existence of angels a truth of faith and teaches that the fall of the angels was a free and irrevocable choice.

Modern theology divided sharply. Friedrich Schleiermacher, in The Christian Faith (1821 to 1822), argued that the idea of the devil should not be a permanent element of Christian doctrine, and Rudolf Bultmann's essay New Testament and Mythology (1941) treated spirits and demons as part of an ancient worldview to be reinterpreted. Karl Barth, in Church Dogmatics III/3 (1950), wrote at length on angels as God's messengers while insisting that demons deserve only a brief, sharp glance. Gustaf Aulén's Christus Victor (English 1931) revived the early church's picture of the atonement as Christ's victory over the powers. Hendrikus Berkhof's Christ and the Powers (1953) and Walter Wink's trilogy (Naming the Powers, 1984; Unmasking the Powers, 1986; Engaging the Powers, 1992) read Paul's powers in relation to the structures and institutions of human life. C. S. Lewis's The Screwtape Letters (1942) warned in its preface against two opposite errors, disbelief in devils and an excessive, unhealthy interest in them. The missiologist Paul Hiebert's essay The Flaw of the Excluded Middle (1982) argued that Western Christianity had lost the vocabulary for the spiritual realm that most of the world's believers take for granted, and the growth of Pentecostal and charismatic churches, especially in Africa, Asia, and Latin America, has made deliverance ministry common. Clinton Arnold's Powers of Darkness (1992) and Michael Heiser's The Unseen Realm (2015) renewed evangelical study of the biblical texts.

differ.view: The sons of God in Genesis 6
differ.body: Three readings have long stood side by side. The angelic reading, found in 1 Enoch, Justin Martyr, and many early fathers and held by many modern commentators, takes ‘sons of God’ in its sense in Job (Job 1:6; 38:7) and connects the passage with the angels who sinned in 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6. The Sethite reading, held by Julius Africanus, Augustine, John Chrysostom, and John Calvin, takes the sons of God as the godly line of Seth intermarrying with the line of Cain, noting that Jesus says angels do not marry (Matthew 22:30) and that the judgment that follows falls on humanity. The royal reading, found in some Jewish interpretation and argued by Meredith Kline among others, takes them as ancient rulers claiming divine status and seizing women. Each reading claims support in the text and its setting, and none is a test of faith.

differ.view: The identity of the angel of the LORD
differ.body: Many early fathers, beginning with Justin Martyr, and many later theologians, especially in the Reformed tradition, identify the angel of the LORD with the Word, the Son of God before his incarnation, since the angel speaks as God, bears God's name (Exodus 23:21), and accepts Joshua's reverence (Joshua 5:14-15). Augustine and many others argue that the angel is a created messenger who speaks with God's full authority, as a herald speaks in the first person for his king, noting that the New Testament says the law was given through angels (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19) and that Hebrews 1 sets the Son above every angel. A third view treats the phrase as a way of speaking of God's own visible presence without further identifying it. All three confess the full deity of Christ; the question is how the Old Testament appearances should be read.

The traditional view, held by the fathers and by most interpreters today such as Clinton Arnold, takes Paul's rulers and authorities as personal spiritual beings, real agents of evil who work through idols, deception, and human sin. Hendrikus Berkhof read them as created structures of human life such as tradition, morality, and the state that God made for good and that have become enslaving when they claim ultimate loyalty. Walter Wink argued that the powers are the inner spiritual reality of institutions and systems, which can be redeemed as well as resisted. Many interpreters hold that Scripture speaks of personal spiritual beings who work through human structures, so that spiritual conflict includes both prayer against evil spirits and resistance to injustice.

differ.view: The divine council and territorial spirits
differ.body: Some scholars, notably Michael Heiser, read Deuteronomy 32:8, Psalm 82, and Daniel 10 together as teaching that God assigned the nations to lesser spiritual beings who rebelled, so that the gospel's spread is a reclaiming of the nations from those powers. Some in the charismatic movement, notably C. Peter Wagner, built on such texts a practice of identifying and confronting spirits over particular places, which they called strategic-level spiritual warfare. Other interpreters read Psalm 82 as addressing unjust human judges, as Jesus' use of it in John 10:34-35 may suggest, and caution that Daniel 10 describes what an angel reports rather than commanding believers to engage territorial spirits. They note that the New Testament's instructions for spiritual conflict center on faith, the word, prayer, and holy living.

Pentecostal and charismatic Christians, and many churches in the majority world, practice deliverance ministry, casting out demons in Jesus' name as he and his apostles did (Mark 16:17 is often cited, though that passage is absent from the earliest manuscripts; Acts 16:18 is not in doubt). The Roman Catholic Church reserves formal exorcism to priests authorized by a bishop and requires careful discernment, including medical assessment. Many Reformed and other evangelicals hold that a believer indwelt by the Holy Spirit cannot be possessed by a demon, though he can be tempted and attacked, and they stress the ordinary means of grace. Christians in these traditions differ over whether believers can be ‘demonized’ and how deliverance should be practiced, while all affirm Christ's authority over every evil power.

errors:
The church has rejected any teaching that makes the devil God's equal or evil an independent power. Manichaeism, which taught two eternal principles of light and darkness, and the dualism attributed to Priscillian were condemned, most explicitly by the First Council of Braga (561) and the Fourth Lateran Council (1215): the devil was created good and became evil by his own will. Scripture never presents history as an undecided contest; Satan acts within limits (Job 1:12) and his end is fixed (Revelation 20:10). The church has also rejected the worship and invocation of angels. Paul warned against it (Colossians 2:18), the angel in Revelation refused it (Revelation 22:9), and the regional Council of Laodicea in the later fourth century forbade Christians to leave the church's worship to invoke angels. Scripture also forbids seeking contact with spirits through mediums and divination (Deuteronomy 18:10-12). The popular idea that people become angels when they die finds no support in Scripture, which distinguishes “myriads of angels” from “the spirits of the righteous made perfect” (Hebrews 12:22-23). Denying the reality of spiritual beings altogether departs from what the church has always confessed about things invisible.

The practical distortions are often more harmful. One sees demons behind every difficulty and neglects human responsibility, ordinary wisdom, and medical care; mental illness in particular has been mistaken for possession, sometimes with cruel results, and people in distress need doctors as well as prayer. Another blames the devil for one's own sin, though Scripture says each is tempted by his own desire (James 1:14). A third feeds a fearful fascination with the dark that the New Testament never encourages; Jesus told his disciples not to rejoice that spirits submit to them but that their names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). The opposite error, a practical disbelief that treats the New Testament's warnings as outdated, leaves believers unprepared for the deception and accusation Scripture says they will face.
life:
The doctrine gives courage. Elisha's frightened servant was shown that “those who are with us are more than those who are with them” (2 Kings 6:16), and Hebrews says God's angels are sent to serve those who will inherit salvation. A believer is not alone in the dark and does not face evil on equal terms. The decisive battle has been won at the cross, where Christ disarmed the powers and freed people from the fear of death. Christian worship joins a larger company: when the church sings the song of the seraphim, “Holy, holy, holy,” it joins “myriads of angels” around God's throne (Hebrews 12:22).

The doctrine also calls for sober watchfulness without fear. The devil is a liar and an accuser, and his typical work is deception, temptation, and accusation: persuading people that God is not good, that sin is harmless, or that they are beyond forgiveness. The New Testament's answer is plain and ordinary: submit to God, resist the devil, hold to the truth, pray, confess sin, and stand with the church. When accusation comes, believers can answer it as Zechariah's vision did, with the grace of God who has chosen and cleansed them. Anyone troubled by fear of the demonic should seek out a trusted pastor and, where needed, medical help, and remember that the one who is in Christ belongs to the one who has already triumphed.
questions: Job 1 and Luke 22 both show Satan acting only with God's permission. How does that shape the way Christians should think about temptation and suffering?
Ephesians 6 describes the armor of God as truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, salvation, the word, and prayer. Why do you think Paul describes spiritual conflict in such ordinary terms?

Jesus told his disciples not to rejoice that spirits submitted to them but that their names were written in heaven. What does that suggest about how much attention Christians should give to the devil and demons?
